# OPENING: Christ had no human biological father

**Position.** [L4] Jesus Christ had no human biological father. His conception in Mary was the work of the Holy Ghost, apart from any man. Joseph was his legal and reputed father, not his begetter. By "biological father" I mean the man whose seed begets the child. The topic asks whether such a man stands behind Christ. The KJV text answers no.

---

## 1. The text names the source of the conception, and it is not a man

**[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The Greek is *ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of the Holy Spirit." The preposition *ek* (out of, from as source) names origin. The same verse fixes the timing: *prin ē synelthein autous*, "before they came together." The pregnancy preceded any union of Joseph and Mary.

**[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** "Conceived" is *gennēthen*, from *gennaō* (to beget, to bring into being). This is the same verb the genealogy uses for fathers begetting sons. In Matthew 1:20 its source is *ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of the Holy Spirit." Where the genealogy has a man as the source, this verse has the Holy Ghost.

**[L3] Matthew 1:2:** "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob." Here *gennaō* has a human father as source. Matthew 1:20 uses the same verb with a different source.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 each give a source for the conception, and both give the Holy Ghost. Matthew 1:2 shows that when Matthew means a human father he says "begat." Where he means this child's conception he names the Holy Ghost. The chain runs from the source named in 1:18, to the source named in 1:20, to the verb's ordinary use in 1:2.

---

## 2. The genealogy breaks its own pattern at Joseph

**[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Every earlier link uses the active *egennēsen*, "begat." The final link switches to the passive *egennēthē*, "was born." The relative pronoun *hēs* ("of whom") is feminine singular, so it points to Mary alone. It cannot point to Joseph. Joseph is called *ton andra Marias*, "the husband of Mary."

**[L3] Matthew 1:12:** "Jechonias begat Salathiel." This is the pattern of "begat" that Matthew 1:16 leaves at Joseph.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:16 carries the line in two ways. It stops using "begat" for the last link, and it makes Mary the one "of whom" Jesus was born. Joseph is placed in the line as husband, not as begetter.

---

## 3. Mary was a virgin, and she says she knew no man

**[L1] Luke 1:27:** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary."

**[L2]** The word is *parthenos* (a virgin). It is used twice in this one verse.

**[L1] Luke 1:34:** "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (to know, including carnal knowledge) is in the present tense: *andra ou ginōskō*, "I know not a man." Her question is about the way, since she has not known a man.

**[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Episkiazō* (to overshadow) is the word for the Highest's power covering her. The conclusion is introduced by *dio kai*, "therefore also." The child is called the Son of God because of this act of the Holy Ghost.

**[L4]** Mary asks how it can be when she knows no man. The answer names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and it gives no man. Luke 1:35 ties the child's identity ("therefore") to that cause and not to a human father.

---

## 4. Prophecy: the sign was a virgin conceiving

**[L1] Matthew 1:22-23:** "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."

**[L1] Isaiah 7:14:** "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L2]** The Hebrew behind the KJV's "virgin" in Isaiah 7:14 is *'almah* (H5959). The Greek in Matthew 1:23 is *parthenos* (a virgin).

**[L3] Genesis 24:43:** "behold, I stand by the well of water; and it shall come to pass, that when the virgin cometh forth to draw water." The KJV uses "virgin" here for *'almah*, of Rebekah, whom Genesis 24:16 calls "a virgin, neither had any man known her."

**[L4]** The KJV renders Isaiah 7:14 as "a virgin shall conceive." Matthew 1:22 says "all this was done" to fulfil it. That is two lines of footing for a conception in a virgin and without a man.

---

## 5. The body was prepared by God

**[L1] Hebrews 10:5:** "Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me."

**[L2]** *Katartizō* (to fit, to prepare) is the word for the preparing of the body. The preparer is God, the one addressed.

**[L3] John 1:14:** "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."

**[L4]** Hebrews 10:5 names God as preparer of the body. John 1:14 says the Word was "made flesh." Neither verse supplies a human father, and both are consistent with Luke 1:35.

---

## 6. Objections the text answers

**Objection A: "His father and mother" (Luke 2:48, and John 6:42).**
**[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
**[L2]** The Greek is *hōs enomizeto*, "as was supposed," from *nomizō* (to deem, to hold by custom or opinion). Luke marks "son of Joseph" as the common opinion and not as fact. John 6:42 ("whose father and mother we know") is the speech of the crowd, which is the same supposition.
**[L3] Luke 2:49:** "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" Mary said "thy father," and the child answered with "my Father" in the next verse, pointing to God.
**[L4]** Luke 3:23 itself marks "son of Joseph" as supposed, and Luke 2:49 corrects the language of the household.

**Objection B: "knew her not till" (Matthew 1:25).**
**[L1] Matthew 1:25:** "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
**[L2]** *Heōs* (until) states the limit of the matter Matthew is addressing, which is the birth. Joseph "knew her not" through the pregnancy.
**[L3] Matthew 1:18:** the child was conceived "before they came together."
**[L4]** Matthew 1:25 confirms that the conception was not Joseph's. The birth came first, and the marriage came after.

**Objection C: Jesus is "of the seed of David."**
**[L1] Romans 1:3:** "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
**[L2]** *Genomenou ek spermatos Dauid*: "made out of the seed of David." The verb is *ginomai* (to become). It does not say "begotten by."
**[L3] Luke 1:32:** "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David."
**[L4]** Luke 1:27 puts Mary and Joseph both "of the house of David," and Matthew 1:16 says Jesus was born "of whom," Mary. Davidic descent through Mary needs no human father.

---

DECLARED CHAIN

1. The Holy Ghost, and not a man, is named as the source of the conception, and the pregnancy came before Joseph and Mary came together. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18 and Matthew 1:20; [L2] *ek pneumatos hagiou* (out of the Holy Spirit) and *gennēthen* (begotten, conceived); [L3] Matthew 1:2, where *gennaō* has a human father as its source.
2. The genealogy ends with a break: Joseph is "the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus," not the one who begat. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:16; [L2] *egennēthē* (was born, passive) against *egennēsen* (begat, active), and *hēs* (of whom, feminine); [L3] Matthew 1:12, "Jechonias begat Salathiel."
3. Mary was a virgin who knew no man, and the angel's answer names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest as the cause. Footing: [L1] Luke 1:27, Luke 1:34, Luke 1:35; [L2] *parthenos* (a virgin), *ginōskō* (to know), *episkiazō* (to overshadow); [L3] Matthew 1:25, "knew her not."
4. The prophecy of a virgin conceiving is applied to this birth. Footing: [L1] Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:22-23; [L2] *'almah* (H5959) rendered "virgin" in the KJV, and *parthenos* (a virgin); [L3] Genesis 24:43.
5. "Son of Joseph" is the supposition of the people, and the child himself names God as his Father. Footing: [L1] Luke 3:23 and Luke 2:49; [L2] *enomizeto* (was supposed) from *nomizō* (to deem by custom); [L3] John 6:42, where the crowd says "whose father and mother we know."
6. Therefore Christ had no human biological father: his conception was of the Holy Ghost in the virgin Mary, and Joseph was his father only by legal and reputed standing. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35; [L2] *ek* (out of) with *gennēthen* (begotten) and *episkiazō* (to overshadow); [L3] Hebrews 10:5, "a body hast thou prepared me."

# ROUND 2: The defender answers the question, concedes one row, and meets each press

## 0. A correction on my own opening

[L1] Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name [was] Mary."

[L2] The phrase "of the house of David" follows *anēr* (G435, a man, husband) and the name *Iōsēph* (G2501, Joseph). It stands with the man.

[L4] My opening said Luke 1:27 puts Mary "of the house of David". The verse does not carry that, and I withdraw the sentence. Mary's descent now rests on the chain in section 1 below, not on Luke 1:27. The withdrawn sentence was a side remark in Objection C, not a declared link.

---

## 1. The question: how is it evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda?

[L1] Hebrews 7:14: "For [it is] evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda."

[L1] Numbers 1:18: "they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names."

[L2] H1004 *bayith* (house, family) and H1 *'ab* (father) stand in Numbers 1:18, a register by "the number of the names". It counts names by house and does not test a begetting.

**Route one: the register through Joseph's house.**

[L1] Luke 2:4: "because he was of the house and lineage of David."

[L1] Luke 2:5: "To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child."

[L1] Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus."

[L1] Matthew 1:21: "thou shalt call his name JESUS." Matthew 1:25: "and he called his name JESUS."

[L4] The register puts the child in Joseph's house by the two things the rows give. Joseph is "of the house and lineage of David" (Luke 2:4), and Joseph names the child (Matthew 1:21, 1:25). The same angel addresses him as "Joseph, thou son of David" (Matthew 1:20) in the very sentence that tells him to take Mary. Matthew's line puts Jesus at the end of "Jacob begat Joseph" (Matthew 1:16). The count by "the house of their fathers" (Numbers 1:18) is a count of names entered, and Joseph's naming enters this one.

**Route two: the flesh through the one he was born of.**

[L1] Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."

[L2] *Ginomai* (G1096, to become, to be made) is the verb. It is not *gennaō* (G1080, to procreate).

[L1] Luke 1:35: "that holy thing which shall be born of thee."

[L4] The rows name one human source for the child's flesh: Mary, "of whom" (Matthew 1:16) and "of thee" (Luke 1:35). Romans 1:3 says that flesh was "of the seed of David". If his flesh is of David's seed, it comes by the human parent the rows name for it. This is my inference from Matthew 1:16, Luke 1:35 and Romans 1:3, and I flag it as an inference. Mary's tribe is the premise it carries, and I hold that premise only as inferred from those three rows.

---

## 2. Answers to the presses

### D1: "of the Holy Ghost" as believers' language

[L1] Matthew 1:18: "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

[L2] The words behind "with child" are *en gastri echousa* (G1064 *gastēr*, womb; G2192 *echō*, to have). The Spirit is named as source of what is in the womb.

[L1] 1 John 5:1: "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God."

[L3] John 3:6: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."

[L4] The vocabulary is shared, but the referent differs by context. In 1 John 5:1 the birth follows from "believeth". In John 3:6 two births stand side by side, one "of the flesh" and one "of the Spirit". In Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 the Spirit is source of "that which is conceived in her", a pregnancy found before any coming together. Of no believer is it written that he was "found with child of the Holy Ghost".

[L2] G1080 *gennaō* is glossed "to procreate (properly, of the father, but by extension of the mother)". In Matthew 1:20, *gennēthen ek pneumatos hagiou* (begotten out of the Holy Spirit) puts the Spirit where the verb properly puts the father.

[L1] John 1:13: "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."

[L4] John 1:13 itself sets "of God" against "of blood... of the will of man". Applied to Matthew 1:20, it gives the Spirit as source in place of the man.

**On "before they came together" (Matthew 1:18).**

[L2] G4905 *synerchomai* is glossed "to convene... or (specially), cohabit (conjugally)". G4250 *prin* means "before".

[L1] Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."

[L3] Deuteronomy 22:23: "If a damsel [that is] a virgin be betrothed unto an husband, and a man find her in the city, and lie with her."

[L4] *Prin synelthein* (before they came together) dates the pregnancy before the conjugal union. Joseph's response in 1:19 is the response of a man who saw a betrothed woman with child and had not known her himself. A husband who had known her would have had no cause to be "minded to put her away". Deuteronomy 22:23, which the challenger cites, describes the case of a betrothed virgin lain with by "a man". The angel's answer in Matthew 1:20 is "fear not... for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost". The "for" gives the reason for not fearing, and the reason is the source of the conception.

**On Matthew 1:25 against C5.**

[L1] Genesis 4:1: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived."

[L1] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

[L2] G1097 *ginōskō* (to know) is the verb in both.

[L4] By the challenger's own canon (Genesis 4:1: knew, then conceived), Matthew 1:25 puts the verb in the negative for the whole time from the taking (1:24) to the birth. Matthew 1:18 dates the conception earlier, "before they came together". The chain from 1:18 to 1:25 therefore has Joseph's "knew her not" standing over the whole pregnancy.

### D2: the passive at Matthew 1:16

[L1] Luke 1:13: "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son."

[L3] Matthew 1:3: "Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar." Matthew 1:5: "Booz begat Obed of Ruth."

[L2] G1080 *gennaō* in Matthew 1:3 and 1:5 is active, with the father as subject and the mother after *ek* (out of).

[L4] The challenger's Luke 1:13 does not meet the pattern in Matthew's own genealogy. When Matthew names a mother, the father keeps the active verb: "Booz begat Obed of Ruth". At Matthew 1:16 the formula is not "Joseph begat Jesus of Mary". It becomes "Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus". The father's active verb stops, the husband title appears, and the feminine "of whom" carries the birth. The break stands in Matthew 1:16 itself, measured against Matthew 1:3 and 1:5.

### D3: Luke 1:35 and "therefore"

[L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

[L2] G4459 *pōs* means "how, in what way".

[L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

[L3] Luke 1:37: "For with God nothing shall be impossible."

[L4] Luke 1:35 is the answer to a question of way, "How shall this be?". It names the Holy Ghost's coming and the Highest's power. Luke 1:37 gives the reason as "with God nothing shall be impossible", which is the language of a wonder. The *dio kai* (therefore also) follows the two clauses of 1:35 directly. The title "Son of God" is tied to them.

[L1] Acts 1:8: "the Holy Ghost is come upon you."

[L1] Luke 9:34: "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them."

[L2] G1904 *epérchomai* (to come upon) and G1982 *episkiázō* (to overshadow) are the same verbs.

[L4] The verbs do not decide the result. At Acts 1:8 the result is power and witnessing, and at Luke 9:34 it is fear. In Luke 1:35 the result clause follows: "that holy thing which shall be born of thee". Here the same agent is named in a sentence whose result is a child, and "of thee" is the human source it names for that birth.

### D4: Isaiah 7:14 and 8:3

[L1] Isaiah 7:11: "Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above."

[L2] H226 *'ôwth* (a sign, a miracle, a prodigy) is the word in Isaiah 7:14. H5959 *'almah* is the word rendered "virgin".

[L1] Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."

[L2] G3933 *parthénos* (a virgin) is the Greek word at Matthew 1:23.

[L1] Isaiah 8:3: "And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son. Then said the LORD to me, Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz."

[L4] Isaiah 7:11 sets the range of the sign as the depth or the height. Isaiah 8:3 gives a different child, called Mahershalalhashbaz and not Immanuel, by a woman called "the prophetess", not "a virgin". Matthew 1:22 uses *plēroō* (G4137, to fulfil) of "all this" and then quotes "a virgin shall be with child" at 1:23. The fulfilment named is the virgin conceiving. Deuteronomy 22:23 shows a betrothed virgin can have a husband, but it states her status "be betrothed", and Matthew 1:18 puts the pregnancy before the union.

### D5: "thy father" and "my Father"

[L1] Luke 2:48: "behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."

[L1] Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

[L1] Luke 2:50: "And they understood not the saying which he spake unto them."

[L4] The child answers "thy father" with "my Father's business". Luke 2:50 says the saying was not understood, so the household's word and the child's word are not the same word. The Solomon case in 1 Chronicles 28:6 ("I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father") shows God taking as son a man whose father was David. In Luke 2:49 the child names God as the Father whose business is his.

**The four voices.**

[L1] Luke 2:33: "Joseph and his mother marvelled."

[L1] Luke 2:43: "the child Jesus tarried behind in Jerusalem; and Joseph and his mother knew not of it."

[L4] In the narrator's own voice at Luke 2:33 and 2:43, the man is named "Joseph" and the woman "his mother". The narrator gives the man his own name, and the same narrator writes at Luke 3:23 "as was supposed" over "the son of Joseph". Luke 2:41 "his parents" is the household's joint term for the two who reared him, and it sits in the same chapter as the narrator's naming of Joseph.

[L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

[L1] John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I came down from heaven?"

[L2] G3543 *nomizō* (to deem, to hold by custom) is the verb in Luke 3:23. The KJV renders it "supposed".

[L4] The KJV's own rendering at Luke 3:23, "as was supposed", is the narrator's mark on "son of Joseph". Acts 16:13's "was wont" (*enomizeto*) is a custom held in common opinion, which is the same register. John 6:42 gives the crowd's claim to know the child's parents, joined with an objection to his saying "I came down from heaven".

### D6: Hebrews 2 and the prepared body

[L1] Hebrews 2:14: "the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same."

[L3] Luke 3:38: "which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God."

[L4] I agree that the child had flesh and blood. The text says he "took part of the same" (Hebrews 2:14) and was "made like unto [his] brethren" in all things (Hebrews 2:17). The first of the line, Adam, is "the son of God" (Luke 3:38) with flesh and no earthly begetter. Likeness of nature (Hebrews 2:14, 2:17) therefore does not require a human begetter. Hebrews 10:5, "a body hast thou prepared me", names the preparer, and Luke 1:35 names the way.

### On C1

[L1] Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne."

[L2] G450 *anístēmi* (to raise up) names God's act of raising up.

[L4] I grant the promise runs from David's flesh to Christ. Route two above answers how, through the one "of whom" he was born (Matthew 1:16) and "of thee" (Luke 1:35). That flesh is "of the seed of David" (Romans 1:3). I hold that the line from David's flesh to Christ's flesh runs through Mary, with no human begetter between.

---

## 3. Question to the challenger

[L1] Matthew 1:19: "Joseph her husband... was minded to put her away privily."

[L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

If Joseph was the one who had known her, what is the "fear" the angel answers in Matthew 1:20, and why does the reason the angel gives in the "for" clause name the Holy Ghost as the source of what is conceived?
